scripts.opening:opening:
[mysteriously] Ghosts of Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] An autumn night in 1904. The gas lamps are lit and the carriages are home. [short pause] This is Millionaire's Row, where mansions for George Pullman, Marshall Field, John J. Glessner and Philip Armour stand shoulder to shoulder, and where the richest families in Chicago lock their doors at night against everyone but their ghosts.

[short pause] Seven stops, on foot, from the corner of Eighteenth Street south to 1919 Prairie. [short pause] You will meet a battlefield under the pavement, a tycoon sealed in concrete, an architect who never saw his masterpiece, a widow who rattles the windows, a man who walked into the lake, and a gunshot nobody has explained. [short pause] The stories are legends, told by ghost tours and by the Glessner House Museum itself. [short pause] The deaths behind them are real.

[short pause] Mind the shadows. Start where the street starts: on the battle ground of 1812.
scripts.stop:battle-ground: [mysteriously] Prairie at Eighteenth, after dark. [short pause] Before the mansions there were sand hills here, and on 15 August 1812 the Battle of Fort Dearborn was fought across them. [short pause] The dead 'lay in the sand, half buried where they were killed, until 1816', and for a century a big cottonwood marked the spot. [short pause] A Tribune writer swore in 1900 that the Pullman house in front of you 'stands about where the massacre took place'. [short pause] George Pullman knew it: in 1893 he set up a bronze of the Potawatomi chief Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm near this corner. According to legend the fallen still walk here on clear, cold nights. [short pause] 'The Americans go searching for their families and friends while the Natives continue to patrol their land.' The man who put up that statue is not walking anywhere. [short pause] His family made sure of it.
scripts.stop:pullman: [mysteriously] 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house. [short pause] George Pullman made his first fortune lifting Chicago out of its own mud, jacking up whole buildings 'on average six feet without causing them any damage'. [short pause] Then came the sleeping car, and Lincoln's body rode home to Springfield in one while 'hundreds of thousands of people lined the route in homage'. [short pause] In 1894 he cut his workers' pay but 'he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman', his company town, and his workers struck. When he died in 1897 his family feared he would be dug up. [short pause] So, the story goes, he went into a 'lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete', with steel rails 'bolted together at right angles' on top. Mrs. Pullman still lives here; the house is razed in 1922. [short pause] And her husband hated the house across the street.
scripts.stop:glessner: [mysteriously] 1800 Prairie, Glessner House, the granite fortress Pullman meant when he grumbled, 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'. [short pause] Its architect, Henry Hobson Richardson, died on 26 April 1886, five weeks before building began on 1 June. He never saw it built. According to legend he came to see it anyway. [short pause] The family felt a presence; cold spots creep into warm rooms; 'If you're lucky, you might catch the man's spirit standing on that same staircase.' One later visitor called it a 'pleasant presence'. [short pause] Pleasant is not a word for the Glessners' daughter Frances's hobby: she grew up to build tiny, perfect dollhouses of real deaths, the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, still used to train detectives. Now turn around. [short pause] The house across the avenue is rattling.
scripts.stop:kimball: [mysteriously] 1801 Prairie, the Kimball house, all steep slate and turret. [short pause] William W. Kimball started in 1857 'beginning with only four pianos' and built a factory 'churning out around 100 pianos and organs every week'. He and his wife Evaline filled the entry hall with Old Master paintings. [short pause] This winter the music stops: he 'died at his home in Chicago on December 16, 1904'. Evaline lived on here until 1921, and in her last years, it is said, she held receptions for 'empty rooms she thought were full of visitors'. [short pause] Today the paintings hang in the Art Institute, and the big north windows shake and rattle when there is no wind at all. The house museum itself asks, 'Could it be that the spirit of Evaline Kimball has returned to the house'. [short pause] Looking for her pictures, maybe. [short pause] Next, a family with a sadder story.
scripts.stop:keith: [mysteriously] 1900 Prairie, Elbridge G. Keith's house, its mansard roof black against the sky. [short pause] A few doors south, at 1906, lives the widow of his brother Edson, the merchant. Edson Keith had not slept properly in ten years. [short pause] Early on Monday 21 September 1896 he slipped out of his house, walked to the lake at the foot of 16th Street, and walked in; the papers reported that he 'committed suicide Monday morning by drowning himself in Lake Michigan'. [short pause] He never came home. Or did he? Ghost hunters say 'his ghost has been seen at his brother's house, where he sometimes appears in the windows.' Look up at the dark panes as you pass. [short pause] Across the avenue, the richest man in Chicago is asleep.
scripts.stop:field: [mysteriously] 1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's house. [short pause] 'Give the lady what she wants', said the merchant, and the ladies made him 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', worth $125 million by 1905. Tonight it all looks safe. It is not. [short pause] In thirteen months his son, next door, will be shot. Six weeks after that, Field plays golf on New Year's Day 1906 with Robert Todd Lincoln, Abraham's son, catches pneumonia and dies on 16 January. [short pause] Father and son, both gone in one winter. The house lasts until 1955, then it is razed too. [short pause] Walk on to the son's house, the one with the footsteps.
scripts.stop:field-jr: [mysteriously] 1919 Prairie, Marshall Field Jr.'s house, with its huge new Burnham addition. [short pause] On Wednesday 22 November 1905 a shot goes off upstairs. He dies five days later at Mercy Hospital, saying 'I shot myself with that revolver – accidentally', and the coroner agrees. Chicago does not. [short pause] Reporters are tipped that he spent the evening at the Everleigh Club, a brothel a few blocks west on Dearborn Street; 'The most popular story is that he was in fact shot at the Everleigh Club' and carried home to make it look like an accident. [short pause] Nobody ever proved it. But later owners heard footsteps echo through empty halls and 'strange cries in the dead of night'. One family reportedly called in an exorcist to clear a spirit that 'sours the air around it'. [short pause] Some houses keep their secrets. [short pause] This one keeps its ghost.
scripts.ending:finish:
[mysteriously] End of the walk at 1919 Prairie. One more ghost, for the road. [short pause] Years later the Clarke House, 'purported to be the city's oldest standing house' and 'twice relocated', will come back to this neighbourhood, and in the park beside it, they say, a woman in a settler's dress drifts among the bushes after dark, while carriage horses clip past that 'always seem to have their bits, but never their harnesses'.

[short pause] Sleep well, Prairie Avenue.
